title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1RC0RB_0RD1LF_1LE1RE_1LA---_1RA0LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1RC0RB_0RD1LF_1LE1RE_1LA---_1RA0LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this machine halts from blank tape. Its run is built from doubling chains, like the Collatz-like sibling 1RB---_1RC1LE_0RD0RF_0RE0LA_1LF0LB_1LA1LD: a block of 1s at the right end doubles again and again, paid for by a run of 10 pairs on its left, until the pairs run out. One chain step is a Lean theorem for all sizes; the bookkeeping at the end of a chain, which involves a whole stack of pair runs, is only observed.
verdict: The question is open. One step of a doubling chain is proved in Lean for every size and every tape further left, and the chain rule matches all 776 chain steps of the first 109 steps. What a chain does when its pairs run out depends on the stack of pair runs further left and is not yet a map.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 9,158 cells have been visited and 4,948 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.05·10<sup>20</sup> steps (accelerated run)
claims.text: The run-length simulator tools/py/bbtools/rleaccel.py (blocks of 2 cells, runs crossed in one step, and cycle jumps, each used only after its one-cycle rule has been proved symbolically for all lengths; tested cell for cell against direct runs) runs 227,000,000 macro steps from blank tape without a halt. That is more than 1.05·1020 machine steps; the tape then spans 55,996,144 cells.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/power
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.284). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.348).

claims.title: One doubling step, for all parameters
claims.text: For every tape L and all K, j: L (10)^(K+2j+5) 1^(4j+2) A>0 reaches L (10)^K 1^(8j+16) A>0, and L (10)^(K+2j+5) 1^(4j+4) A>0 reaches L (10)^K 1^(8j+22) A>0; the start of a chain, L (10)^(k+1) 0 1^5 A>0, reaches L (10)^k 1^18 A>0. Each step is a start piece, j or j+1 inner cycles (each moves two pairs from the left run into the 1s; chained by an induction written by hand) and an end piece, the pieces proved by bbtools.symtm.

claims.title: The run follows the chain rule
claims.text: Sampling each time the head is in A at the right end on a 0, the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps contain 162 chain starts and 776 chain steps, all as the rule says (no mismatch); the other 406 transitions are chain ends.

claims.title: Chain ends work on a stack of pair runs
claims.text: Left of the last pair run the tape is a list of pair runs separated by markers 1 0 0 or 1 1 0, for example (10)^209 1 (10)^344 0 (10)^32 0 (10)^112 0 1^5 at step 4,999,243. When a chain's pairs run out, the block 1^m is turned back into pairs and runs are merged, split or doubled; the examples show several different cases.

claims.title: A chain end at a 0 marker
claims.text: When the pairs run out at a 0 marker, the marker is absorbed (absorb0), and a second cycle (eat) follows: L (10)^(x+2) C>(10)^(k+1) 110 (1010)^(n+1) R reaches L (10)^x C>(10)^(k+5) 110 (1010)^n R. end0 chains them for t turns, for all parameters and any tapes L, R. The inner cycle is also proved with any tape on the right (cycR). What happens when x or the blocks run out is not proved.

claims.title: How far back the chain ends read
claims.text: Of the 1,506 sample transitions in the first 109 steps, 229 stay in the final ones, 1,015 read into the last pair run, 115 into the run before it, 1 into the third, and 146 reach the left end of the tape. The run passes 51 times through the start of absorb0 and 73 times through an E frame. So the samples are not a finite set of frames, and the whole-tape frame-map method does not apply as it is.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The chain step is proved; the missing piece is a map for the chain ends (a stack machine on the pair runs), and then the halting question for that map, which is probably Collatz-like.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. A block of 1s doubles in chains while a run of 10 pairs pays for it, as in a Collatz-like sibling; the chain step is proved, the end of a chain is still a puzzle.

facts.text: one doubling step, for all sizes and any tape further left, proved in Lean
chain steps in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps that follow the rule
No halt in the C simulator; 9,158 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: A block that doubles while pairs pay for it
html: Write a for the pair 1 0. Look at the run each time the head is in state A at the right end of the tape, on a 0. The tape then ends in a run of pairs and a block of 1s, P a^k 1^m, where P is everything further left.

Most of the time the machine is in a doubling chain: P stays the same and (k, m) goes (k, 5), (k, 11), (k−1, 18), (k−14, 48), (k−41, 110), (k−100, 232), (k−219, 478), … The block grows from m to 2m+12 or 2m+14 (alternately), and each step costs about m/2 pairs. For example at step 90,524 the tape ends in a^164 0 1^5, and the next samples are a^164 1^11, a^163 1^18, a^150 1^48, a^123 1^110, a^64 1^232.

One chain step is a zigzag: the head carries the block of 1s to the right as pairs, then walks back and forth, each round trip moving two pairs from the left run into the 1s and using up two pairs on the right. Lean proves one step for every size and every P.

sections.heading: A stack of pair runs
html: P is itself a list of pair runs with markers between them: 1 0 0 (written 0 below) or 1 1 0 (written 1), for example a^209 1 a^344 0 a^32 0 a^112 0 1^5 at step 4,999,243. When a chain runs out of pairs, the block of 1s is turned back into pairs and the runs near the right end are merged, doubled or split, and a new chain starts. These chain ends come in several kinds, and they are not yet written as a map.

The machine halts when it reads a 1 in state E. In the sibling machine the halt needs a chain to use up its pairs exactly; something similar may hold here, but that is a guess until the chain ends are understood.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.284). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.348).
After 109 steps the tape spans 9,158 cells (364 left of the start, 6,993 right), with a density of 1s of 0.54.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: Collatz-like counters (doubling chains of a unary block over a stack of pair runs)
summary: Runs of 10 pairs separated by markers, and a unary block 1^m at the right end that doubles in chains (m to 2m+12 or 2m+14) while the last pair run pays for it; the chain step is proved in Lean for all parameters, what happens at a chain's end is not yet worked out.
